opus-5.5.text:
I think the influence has been enormous, and honestly a bit complicated. On one hand, large language models have shown everyone what scaling can do. The idea that you can take a fairly simple objective, like next-token prediction, put enormous amounts of data and compute behind it, and get these emergent capabilities has changed how the whole field thinks about research. Many problems we used to treat as separate subfields, each with its own clever tricks, now look like they might be absorbed into one general system.

But for academia this creates real tension. The most visible progress now depends on resources that universities simply don't have: tens of thousands of GPUs, huge proprietary datasets, large engineering teams. A PhD student can't train a frontier model. So there's a kind of identity crisis. Students ask, "If industry labs are doing the big models, what is my research for?" Some people respond by doing prompt engineering or evaluating someone else's API, which can be useful, but I don't think that should be the center of academic research.

My view is that academia's role is not to compete on scale but to ask the questions industry is less incentivized to ask. Industry has to converge; once a recipe works, everyone optimizes it. Academia can afford to diverge. We can ask whether language is really the right foundation for intelligence, or whether there are things that text-based models fundamentally miss: grounding in the physical world, visual understanding, spatial reasoning, how an agent learns from interacting with its environment rather than just reading the internet. As someone working in vision, I think a lot about this. Language is a very compressed, human-made abstraction. The visual world is much richer and messier, and I don't think we've had our "GPT moment" there in the same way.

There's also a cultural influence. LLMs made research much more empirical and engineering-heavy. That's good in some ways; it rewards people who actually make things work. But it can also make the field more homogeneous, with everyone chasing the same benchmarks and the same architecture. Some of the most important ideas in deep learning came from people who were slightly out of fashion at the time. So I'd like academia to protect that space for taste, curiosity, and long-term bets.

So I'd say LLMs have been a wake-up call for academia. They forced us to rethink what kind of research matters. I don't see it as the end of academic AI research, but it does mean we need to be much more deliberate about choosing problems where a small group with a good idea can still change the direction of the field.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, this is something I think about a lot, because I've lived on both sides of it. I spent years at FAIR, and now I'm back in academia at NYU, and the gap between what industry labs can do and what a university lab can do has grown in a way that's hard to ignore.

The most obvious influence is on resources. If you want to train a frontier model today, you need thousands of GPUs, and no university has that. So there's a natural anxiety among students and faculty: if the most important results come from scaling, and we can't scale, what is our role? I hear this from PhD students constantly. They read a paper from OpenAI or Google or DeepMind and feel like the game is already over.

But I actually don't think that's the right way to look at it. I think LLMs have been clarifying for academia, because they've forced us to ask what we're actually good at. We're not good at being a smaller version of an industry lab. We are good at asking questions that industry has no incentive to ask, or doesn't have the patience to ask.

Let me give you a concrete example from my own experience. When we did ConvNeXt, the whole community had more or less decided that transformers had won in vision. Nobody at a big company was going to spend time going back and asking whether convolutional networks were really dead, or whether the comparison had just been unfair. That's a question only someone with a bit of freedom and stubbornness asks. And it turned out the answer was interesting. The same thing with the work on representation learning and diffusion transformers. These weren't about having the most compute. They were about looking carefully at something everyone had stopped looking at.

So I tell my students that our job is to be the people who understand things. Industry is very good at making things work. Academia should be very good at explaining why they work, where they break, and what the next idea is. If you look at the history of this field, the ideas that eventually got scaled usually started small. Attention didn't start as a trillion-parameter experiment.

That said, I don't want to be naive. There are real problems. One is that academia has been pushed toward benchmark chasing, because that's what gets attention, and that's exactly the game we can't win. Another is talent. A lot of the best students go to industry right away, which is their right, but it thins out the ecosystem. And a third is that we've become dependent on models we can't inspect. If you're doing research on top of an API, you're not really doing science on the model. You're doing science on a black box that might change next month.

So the way I see it, LLMs haven't made academia irrelevant. They've made it harder, and they've made us more honest about what we're for. The labs that will do well are the ones that stop trying to compete on scale and start competing on understanding, on new paradigms, on the questions that are too risky or too slow for a company roadmap. That's always been the point of a university. We just forgot it for a few years.

astra-6.text:
I think the influence is huge, and it creates a real tension for academia. On one hand, large language models have opened up so many interesting research questions. On the other hand, the resources needed to train these systems make it difficult for most academic labs to participate at the same scale as industry.

The risk is that we start treating scale as the only measure of progress. If academic research becomes a competition to build a slightly smaller version of an industrial model, we’re limiting what universities can contribute. Academia needs room to question the assumptions behind the dominant approach—to ask what these models actually learn, where they fail, and whether there are more efficient ways to achieve the same capabilities.

So I see this as an opportunity to rethink the role of academic research. We can study questions that don’t have an immediate product payoff, and we can pursue ideas that might look unpromising initially. For students especially, I think it’s important to develop your own judgment about what matters, even when one direction is attracting almost all the attention.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the influence is enormous, and it creates both excitement and some anxiety in academia. Large language models have opened up many interesting research questions, but they also make people ask: if the most visible progress requires huge amounts of compute and data, what role can a university lab play?

My view is that academia shouldn’t simply try to reproduce what a large industrial lab can do with more resources. We need to ask questions that aren’t answered just by making a model bigger. What are these models actually learning? How do we evaluate them properly? Can we find a simpler or more efficient approach? Those are areas where a small team can still make a meaningful contribution.

The concern is that everyone gets pulled toward the same topic and the same measures of success. Students may feel that if they aren’t working on language models, their research is no longer relevant. I don’t think that’s healthy. Academia needs room for different directions, including ideas whose value isn’t immediately obvious. The excitement around language models should expand the questions we ask, rather than narrow them.
